title: Nanomaterials in Paints and Coatings: Know the Risks
summary: Many paints and coatings now contain engineered nanomaterials. Health effects are not well understood, and spraying may exceed recommended exposure limits. Use the same dust and mist controls you already use, and ask what is in the product.
talking_points: Nanomaterials are engineered particles up to 100,000 times thinner than a human hair. Adding them can make paint anti-corrosive, anti-graffiti, anti-microbial, self-cleaning, UV protective, or water repellent.
CPWR has found nearly 1,000 construction products that report nanomaterials. More than half are paints and coatings. Check nano.elcosh.org for the products you use.

OSHA has no exposure standard for nanomaterials. NIOSH has recommended exposure limits for a few, such as carbon nanotubes, carbon nanofibers, titanium dioxide, and silver. NIOSH considers nano-sized titanium dioxide a potential occupational carcinogen.
CPWR tests found that spraying nano paints and coatings may exceed NIOSH limits. Airless spraying is one task that may overexpose you.
Breathing is the main route of exposure. Nanoparticles can reach deep in the lungs and move to other organs. Skin contact and swallowing should not be ignored.
Use local exhaust ventilation and wet methods. Both cut exposure to nanomaterials as they do for larger particles. Good work practices also reduce exposure to bystanders.
Use a respirator when needed. Filters and cartridges that are used correctly do capture nanoparticles.
Safety data sheets often do not list nanomaterials or their hazards. Ask your employer what is in the product.
site_hazards_to_check: Spray painting or sanding in areas without ventilation or local exhaust
Unknown coating products with a missing or incomplete SDS
Bystanders working near spray or sanding
Respirators that are the wrong type, unfit, or with the wrong cartridges
discussion_questions: Do we know if any product we are using today contains nanomaterials?
Which tasks today are most likely to put mist or dust in the air?
What ventilation or respirator controls are in place for these tasks?
